extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political philosophy, history, and legislators/political writers
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and explaining normative definitions and necessary components of political communities (republics/cities), including what counts as citizenship and how terms should be used. The page debates competing senses of 'republic' and lists elements and social roles necessary to a city.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistent use of political terminology
rubrics_metrics.description: "The elements and definitions In most of the arts and sciences are understood alike... but in the science of legislation... there is a confusion of languages, as if men were but lately come from Babel. Scarcely any two writers, much less nations, agree in using words in the same sense."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Page urges that writers and legislators must clarify and consistently define terms (monarchy, aristocracy, democracy, king, prince, lords, commons, nobles, patricians, plebeians). Examples show how the same word (e.g., 'king', 'prince') has different meanings in France, England, Poland, Liege, Venice, Germany, Russia. Anti-pattern: assuming a universal meaning for political words; this hinders mutual understanding of principles and rules of government.

rubrics_metrics.name: Republic defined as government where all are equally subject to the laws
rubrics_metrics.description: "Others again, more rationally, define a republic to signify only a government, in which all men, rich and poor, magistrates and subjects, officers and people, masters and servants, the first citizen and the last, are equally subject to the laws."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author endorses this as 'the true, and only true definition of a republic.' Emphasizes equality before law as the core evaluative criterion for calling a polity a republic. Practical implication: when judging whether a state is a republic, check whether laws equally bind every class and individual.

rubrics_metrics.name: Republic as representative democracy (alternative usage)
rubrics_metrics.description: "The English and French writers ... mean by them a democracy, or rather a representative democracy: a government in one centre, and that centre the nation; that is to say, that centre a single assembly, chosen at stated periods by the people, and invested with the whole sovereignty — the whole legislative, executive, and judicial power."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes this is a common modern/English-French usage (e.g., Marchamont Nedham). Guidance: be aware of this narrower usage when reading or composing political analysis; flag potential equivocation between the property/equality-based definition and the representative-assembly-centered definition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Res publica (republic) principally concerns the property of the people
rubrics_metrics.description: "Res publica therefore was publica res, the wealth, riches, or property of the people... Res populi ... could be no other than a government, in which the property of the people predominated and governed; and it had more relation to property than liberty."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument: historically and etymologically 'republic' relates to public property; therefore an important criterion for republican government is the security and governance of property by law. This view ties property protection to liberty: property cannot be secure unless individuals are free to acquire/use/dispose of it. Use this criterion when evaluating historical or legal claims about republicanism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seven necessary elements of a city (Portenari/Aristotle enumeration)
rubrics_metrics.description: Portenari (citing Aristotle) lists six (here rendered as seven) necessary things: 1) provisions (food), 2) clothes/habitations/arts, 3) arms (defense), 4) money (commerce/capital), 5) worship (religion), 6) administration of justice and government; and correspondingly seven sorts of men: husbandmen, artificers, soldiers, merchants/capitalists, rich men, priests, and judges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each element is linked to social functions: husbandmen for provisions, artificers for arts/domestic life, soldiers for defense, merchants and capitalists for money, priests for worship, judges/magistrates for government. Use this list as a checklist of functional necessities for a political community. The page also notes these items are instruments for civil life; citation: 'Arist. Polit. lib. vii.' Examples and cross-reference to Portenari are provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doctrine that husbandmen, artificers, and merchants are 'instruments' not citizens (criticized)
rubrics_metrics.description: Portenari/Aristotle's doctrine: husbandmen, artificers, and merchants are only instruments subservient to uses of the city and therefore not 'parts' of the city in the same political sense; they should not be numbered among citizens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author strongly criticizes this exclusion as inhuman and dangerous: it effectively surrenders people to the rule of a few (aristocracy/despotism). Anti-pattern: excluding productive classes from citizenship and political voice. Practical evaluative note: when assessing historical regimes or constitutional rules, examine whether they exclude classes from citizenship rights and judge accordingly (author views such exclusion negatively). The text also notes only a few cantons and England historically allowed such classes civic voice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representative assemblies as remedy for scale and corruption in large states
rubrics_metrics.description: "The ancient method of taking the sense of an assembly of citizens in the capital... was very imperfect, and extremely exposed to corruption: but, since the invention of representative assemblies, much of that objection is removed."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion for institutional design: use representative bodies to aggregate interests of diverse social groups in extensive territories. Representative assemblies mitigate practical impossibility of mass deliberation and reduce corruption/exposure of the old direct-assembly method. Implication: when recommending or evaluating constitutions, consider representation as the means to include farmers, merchants, and artificers in governance for large polities.
